content: This is the discussion thread for #Project announcements > AnnalsChallenge

Is any kind of (I will slightly abuse the term) 'meta-analysis' intended to be performed on the data set itself? A cross-index by subject category or common term translated to Lean expression phrasebook or relation where overlap of basic terms is recorded between data elements or even just a Galois connection between results and cited sources might be of interest. Granted anyone with access to the repo can roll their own, but perhaps such 'meta-analyses' will come later from the people maintaining the challenge? I am not finding mention of such in the announcement or the repo.
sender_full_name: J. J. Issai (project started by GRP)

content: We've certainly kept track of the distribution of papers across subject areas using the publicly available MSC subject classifications. Naturally, some areas (e.g. combinatorics) are better represented in our formalization than others (e.g. partial differential equations). We're planning to run more analyses like these and will discuss these questions in our forthcoming paper.
Is the project open to external contributions? I would be interested to submit some PDE problem statements.

We have our own internal process for formalizing statements in a consistent manner and vetting them carefully, so we aren't accepting external contributions (although corrections are certainly welcome, see the readme).

That being said, part of the goal of this project is to improve mathlib support for these disparate areas of mathematics, and PDEs is certainly an underdeveloped area of mathlib. So I'd suggest picking some PDE problem statements, think about how they would be formalized in an ideal world, and then work on helping mathlib move in that direction. That would be very appreciated!

I second what Thomas is saying. As you can see from the repo, essentially all of the statements are each in one relatively short self-contained file which just imports mathlib. But what is far less visible from the repo alone is all the basic material which was formalised in PRs to mathlib over the last year, which enabled us to make all these short files.

@Joris van Winden let me give you an example or two. The first few PDE papers on our list of currently unformalized statements are https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.07230 , https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.10693 , https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.05583 , https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.07988. How many lines would it take to state the main theorem of one of these papers in Lean, using mathlib? And how many of those lines are definitions which you feel should be in mathlib already? One way that you could help would be by opening PRs to mathlib containing these definitions and API for these definitions.

Is there any marker your team has used in mathlib PRs to identify that they were done in the course of this project (like lots of people put "From project-name" in their PRs to say where the code is coming from)?

No, we haven't been using any such marker (although the mathlib PRs are less "from AnnalsChallenge" and more "for AnnalsChallenge" in the sense that we mostly wrote mathlib PRs directly rather than upstreaming mathlib-suitable code from our repo).
All 50 of these problems are now part of https://lean-lang.org/eval.
